title: Probabilistic Memory Safety Map for Mixed Weight/KV/Activation Workloads
creator: Riley Chen
description: Problem: intermittent OOMs and conservative static reservations across our fleet cause wasted GPU capacity or hard failures when traffic shifts. Continuous batching and diverse model sizes mean the dominant memory consumer shifts between model weights, KV cache (prefix-heavy sessions), and transient activations. We need a robust, automated way to compute per-GPU memory budgets and short-term headroom that balances throughput and safety.
proposal: Introduce a Probabilistic Memory Safety Map (PMSM) service that ingests short-window workload telemetry and outputs a per-GPU memory budget vector (weights | kv | activations | safety_reserve). PMSM uses compact workload fingerprints (model id, sequence length histogram, active-session KV intensity), a Bayesian occupancy estimator to compute tail-memory quantiles, and an explicit safety corridor policy. The scheduler consumes the map to pick batch sizing, kv residency targets, and preemptive eviction thresholds. Map updates occur every 10s–60s depending on volatility.
technical_details: Telemetry: sample per-request payload: model, seq_len, kv_size_estimate, tokens_out, latency bucket (p50/p95), and current memory usage buckets.

Estimator: fit a mixture-of-quantiles model per model-shape/build (weights fixed per model, kv and activations variable). Produce 95th and 99th percentile memory occupation estimates over a sliding window with exponential decay.
Safety corridor: compute safety_reserve = max( min_reserve, quantile(99) - reserved_budget) with configurable conservative multiplier for P0 customers.
Outputs: vector normalized to GPU memory: {weights_reserved, kv_soft_limit, activation_budget, safety_reserve}. Scheduler consumes these to enforce continuous-batching decisions and eviction hints.

Integration: export via internal control-plane API; a new lightweight admission hook in the runtime will check budgets before dequeueing batches and will perform soft-throttles or route to fallback model variants when budgets are exhausted.
Fallbacks: policy to gracefully degrade to smaller model variants, lower batch size, or immediate KV eviction (honoring pinned sessions) when reserve breached.
Rollout: start as opt-in for a small Dedicated pool, run A/B for 3 weeks, then expand to more pools with telemetry gates.
acceptance_criteria: PMSM runs in prod for a pilot pool and emits budgets every 10-60s without causing API slowdowns.
OOM rate in pilot pool decreases by >= 60% relative to baseline during traffic spikes.
Average GPU utilization increases by >= 6% with no increase in customer-visible error rate.
Scheduler honors PMSM budgets and fallback routing is exercised without SLO violations more than 0.1% of requests.
risks_and_tradeoffs: Estimator complexity: overfitting to burst patterns could lead to overly tight reserves and latency P99 regressions.
Telemetry costs: increased metrics cardinality and storage; mitigate with sampling and compact histograms.
Interference: aggressive eviction may impact long-lived pinned sessions; will surface per-customer QoS overrides.
Consistency: short update windows may cause oscillation between throttle and release—introduce damping and hysteresis.
implementation_plan: Week 0–1: instrumentation - add lightweight per-request histograms and kv_intensity estimate in runtime (sampling 1/10).
Week 2: PoC offline estimator using existing telemetry; validate tail estimators against historical OOM incidents.
Week 3–4: implement PMSM service and control-plane API; add admission hook and soft-throttle actions in runtime behind a feature flag.
Week 5–6: run pilot on 2 Dedicated pools; collect OOMs, utilization, and latency metrics; iterate policy multipliers.
Week 7: A/B analysis and safety review; prepare rollout to more pools with documented knobs.
metrics_and_monitoring: KV eviction frequency and percent failed evictions
Request latency p50/p95/p99 for affected models
Number of fallback routing events and their downstream error impact
